content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is concerned with model sparsification. Authors propose an iterative method for dynamic sparsification which iteratively prunes and reactivates some of the weights (or channels, for structured pruning) in the network, balancing the exploitation (train to the best performance, assume stable architecture) and exploration (reactive some of the  weights). The choice of things to prune or add back is guided by (existing) magnitude importance. The experiments on structured and unstructured sparsity problems demonstrate improvements over SOTA. The proposed method exhibits  more stable architecture (e.g. weights that are reactivated don't often get subsequently pruned in later iterations).

content.title: Author response to Reviewer dLrg
content.comment:
We sincerely thank reviewer dLrg for the interests in our paper and detailed comments. Some of the questions raised by reviewer dLrg like novelty of LookAhead and diversity of experiments are already clarified above in our overall response. We now answer the remaining below.

**_Is your whole process: repeat(normal training for some steps + LookAhead) or repeat(LookAhead)?_**

 We thank the reviewers for pointing this out. In short, we repeat LookAhead step to update the sparse architecture until we reach the number of update steps. We have rewritten Section 3 to add clarity in the revised version of the paper. 

**_Ablation of $\mathbf{H, J, K}$ on CIFAR-10?_** 

The period $H,J,K$ are important hyperparameters for LookAhead as they control the balance between exploitation and exploration. We used different sets of $H,J,K$ for CIFAR-10 from those of ImageNet. We added the ablation Table 4 to the Appendix demonstrating the sensitivity of LookAhead to $H, J, K$ on CIFAR-10.

**Reported epochs in Table 1?** 

Indeed, we report the total number of epochs for training in table-1 in the main paper. For the finetuning experiment, this number does also include the epochs required to pretraining the dense model.

**_How is $\Theta_K$ initialized?_** 

$\Theta_K$ is randomly initialized, and we do not impose restrictions on the initialization method or the initial sparsity. Concretely for unstructured weight sparsity, we start with a random selection of sparse weights that matches the target sparsity. For a fair comparison with RigL, we also use the same ERK sparsity distribution and avoid changing this distribution through training by reallocating sparsity across layers.

**_Complexity for pruner/grower solver (constraint optimization)?_** 

We leverage the efficient augmented knapsack solver developed in HALP which also includes the complexity of the solver. Specifically, as shown in detail in Appendix R of HALP, the time complexity of the augmented solver is $O(\sum_{l=1}^L m_l^2\times C)$ with $m_l^2$ representing the number of channels for layer $l$ and $C$ being the latency constraint.

**_Why bolden Pruning-IMP in Table.1?_** 

We compared our approach with other sparsity training methods, that is methods that do not require a pretrain dense model. In contrast, Pruning-Imp starts from a pretrained dense model. In the revised version of the manuscript, Table 1 of the main paper is now organized according to the training cost to facilitate the comparison.

$\text{[1]}$. Wimmer, Paul, Jens Mehnert, and Alexandru Condurache. "Interspace Pruning: Using Adaptive Filter Representations to Improve Training of Sparse CNNs." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022 

$\text{[2]}$. Kim, Jangho, et al. "Dynamic Collective Intelligence Learning: Finding Efficient Sparse Model via Refined Gradients for Pruned Weights." arXiv preprint arXiv:2109.04660 (2021).

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this work, the authors re-formulate network sparsification as an exploitation-exploration process during initial training to enable dynamic sparsification. The exploitation phase assumes architecture stability and trains it to maximize accuracy. Whereas the exploration phase challenges the current architecture with a LookAhead step that reactivates pruned parameters, quickly updates them together with existing
ones, and reconfigures the sparse architecture with a pruning-growing paradigm.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
\+ The method surpasses recent work by +1.3% top-1 accuracy at the same compression ratio for ResNet50-ImageNet unstructured sparsity. Moreover, the structured sparsity results also improve upon the previous hardware-aware pruning method by +0.8% top-1 accuracy.

\- The novelty may be limited. The idea is very similar to the RigL paper. The authors may discuss the difference with RigL. In the RigL paper, it also has a prune and grow process to first remove a fraction of connections and activate new ones, and then train with the updated network. Most of the techniques in each steps are based on previous works, such as cosine decay function from RigL, magnitude or Taylor importance for the importance score, using masks as pruning indicators. I can hardly see something new in this paper.

\- In table 1 and table 2, the baselines are from 2020 or earlier. It is better to compare with more recent baselines. 

\- The FPS in structured pruning can be improved but the improvement is not significant. Besides, I do not understand where the FPS improvements come from. This paper focus on software algorithms. If this method and other methods prune the same number of channels and have equal left channels, why their inference speed differs?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The novelty may be limited. See the weakness. 

In table 1 and table 2, the baselines are from 2020 or earlier. It is better to compare with more recent baselines. 

The writing can be improved. There are some typos such as the sentence after equation (10) in the appendix.

content.title: Author response to All reviewers
content.comment:
Dear Reviewers and ACs,

We sincerely thank all the reviewers for their valuable comments and constructive feedback. Below we provide clarifications to their comments, which have also integrated into the revised version of the manuscript. 

**Novelty of the proposed method and Comparison with RigL and DCIL.**

We want to clarify the differences between our approach and those related methods. As pointed out by the reviewers, LookAhead is close to the family of dynamic sparsity training methods. The main difference relies in the way we conduct the exploration to discover the enhanced sparse structure during training. RigL grows greedily based on instantaneous gradients of small data batches potentially leading to unstable discovered sparse architecture. In contrast, our method explores more solidly with a novel **_Reactivate&Explore_** step that temporarily activates all removed neurons to quickly look ahead the performance after growing.

DCIL is a soft masking based method similar to DPF which relies on estimating gradients on the sparse parameters through STE, which requires two forward and backward passes. In addition, the method requires to compute dense gradients, causing a significant amount of additional compute cost. In contrast, our method deals with a sparse model for most of the time(except the dense forward pass for _Reactivate & Explore_ stage) yielding tremenduous training cost saving, as explained in detail in section A.4 of our revised Appendix.

We have explicitly included these differences in the related work and included additional comparisons in our experiments section of the main paper. In addition, the section _Effectiveness of the exploration strategy_ in the main paper quantifies the differences and the convergence between our method and RigL.

**More recent unstructured weight pruning baselines and training cost comparison.**

 Reviewers suggested adding additional comparisons in the unstructured sparsity experiments. 
Initially, we compared our approach with dynamic sparsity methods as those are the closest ones to our approach. In the revised version, we also included results from DCIL[2] and interspace pruning (CVPR'22)[1] which include the latest SOTA method given a target compression ratio. 

In the revised version of the experiments, we also included the estimated training cost required to obtain the sparse model. 

As we can see in Table 1 of the main paper, for $80\%$ sparsity, our approach beats DCIL with a $+0.9\%$($77.1v.s.76.2$) Top-1 improvement while halving the training cost. For $90\%$ sparsity, our approach achieves comparable Top-1 as IP-FT[1] ($75.7 v.s. 75.8$) with halved training cost. 

**Diversity of Experiments.**

As requested by the reviewers, we have also included an experiment on object detection on the PASCAL VOC dataset in the revised version of the paper. As shown in the new section **_Generalization to Object Detection_**, our approach beats the current SOTA method HALP with a $+1.2$ mAP improvement($78.62 v.s. 77.42$) while requiring much less training cost ($\text{x}0.29v.s.\text{x}1.23$).

**Experiment Specifics Raised by Reviewer dLrg**

 Reviewer dLrg has raised several questions regarding specifics of LookAhead. We address them in individual response to reviewer dLrg. 

$\text{[1]}$. Wimmer, Paul, Jens Mehnert, and Alexandru Condurache. "Interspace Pruning: Using Adaptive Filter Representations to Improve Training of Sparse CNNs." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022 

$\text{[2]}$. Kim, Jangho, et al. "Dynamic Collective Intelligence Learning: Finding Efficient Sparse Model via Refined Gradients for Pruned Weights." arXiv preprint arXiv:2109.04660 (2021).
